experimental_analysis.analysis_report:
Analysis Report — Energy-Adaptive FlashAttention (EA-FA) on NVIDIA T4 (SM75)

1) What we set out to test
- Goal: Demonstrate that the policy-layer edition of EA-FA (Energy-Adaptive FlashAttention) reduces energy-to-solution at accuracy parity versus strong T4 baselines across realistic sequence lengths, following the pre-registered Verification Policy (Experiment Strategy).
- Constraints on T4: DVFS is typically denied; RPA degenerates to kernel/backend/precision policy only. Many Hopper-specific kernel features in the full EA-FA (e.g., TMA, warpgroups power-gating) are not available; the T4 edition focuses on: policy routing between SDPA-math and xFormers MEA, entropy-guided mixed precision promotions (MPTS), and a lightweight sparse-KV skip (SKP).

2) What actually ran (as evidenced by the logs)
- Environment install successful (PyTorch 2.8.0 CU12 stack, xformers 0.0.32.post2, transformers 4.56.0, pynvml 12.0.0).
- A short train/eval workflow was executed (50 train steps), then evaluation with a single run at L≈512 ("Preprocessed ... L512"), eval_batch_size=4, and 12 attention modules replaced by EnergyAwareAttention. This suggests a smaller GPT-style model rather than the pre-registered GPT-2 M/L or OPT-1.3B.
- Evaluated three backends once each: EA_FA_T4, xFormers MEA, SDPA math. No seed grid, no interleaving, no WikiText-103 or LAMBADA reported; the perplexities are very high (~360), consistent with a non-standard or toy dataset.
- No DVFS telemetry or acceptance/denial messages captured in the provided logs (likely denied on T4).

3) Outcomes (as reported)
- Perplexity (PPL):
  • EA_FA_T4: 360.664
  • xFormers MEA: 360.596 (Δ vs EA = −0.068)
  • SDPA math: 360.664 (identical to EA)
- Throughput (tokens/s):
  • EA_FA_T4: 25,253.5
  • xFormers MEA: 41,831.9 (+65.7% vs EA)
  • SDPA math: 25,302.5 (~equal to EA; +0.2%)
- Energy per batch (J):
  • EA_FA_T4: 3.099 J
  • xFormers MEA: 0.906 J (−70.8% vs EA)
  • SDPA math: 2.978 J (−4.1% vs EA)

4) Interpretation against the intended design
- Router behavior: The EA-FA router in code selects xFormers for S ≥ 768; at S=512 it defaults to SDPA. The near-identical tokens/s and PPL for EA vs SDPA indicate EA routed to SDPA and added MPTS/SKP overhead, slightly increasing energy (+4.1%) with no speed gain.
- Baseline dominance at L≈512 on T4: xFormers MEA substantially outperforms both EA and SDPA in energy (−70.8%) and throughput (+65.7%) while maintaining essentially the same PPL (Δ≈0.068). Under the pre-registered equivalence margin (ΔPPL ≤ 0.05), EA matches SDPA exactly but does not meet strict equivalence vs xFormers in this single measurement (though the absolute difference is tiny).
- DVFS: No evidence of granted app clocks in logs; as pre-registered, we do not ascribe any benefit to DVFS. RPA was thus policy-only and provided no gains in this run.
- Component effects (MPTS, SKP): The run did not log promotion/skip rates or ablations, so we cannot quantify component contributions. The only observable effect is small overhead when EA routed to SDPA at short sequence length.

5) Deviations from the pre-registered protocol (threats to validity)
- Coverage: Only one sequence length (≈512), one tiny batch size (4), and one pass per backend were reported; no 5-seed pairing, no interleaving A-B-A-B per batch, no L∈{512,1024,2048} grid, and no model grid (GPT-2 M/L, OPT-1.3B) as planned.
- Datasets/metrics: The planned datasets (WikiText-103, LAMBADA, PG-19) were not reported. PPL values (~360) suggest a non-standard or small corpus; accuracy parity via TOST and numerical RMSE checks were not documented.
- Telemetry and integrity checks: The NVML energy-integration cross-check (<2% discrepancy), throttle reasons, and power/clocks telemetry were not included in the provided snippet. Memory sanity ratios and per-batch diagnostics (promotion/skip rates) were also not present.

6) Conclusions
- On this T4 run at L≈512, EA-FA (policy edition) does not demonstrate a clear advantage. It matches SDPA’s accuracy and throughput but consumes slightly more energy (+4.1%), and it is substantially worse than xFormers MEA in both energy (+242% energy/batch) and throughput (−39.6%).
- The negative outcome is consistent with the router’s current heuristic (choosing SDPA below S=768), the lack of DVFS control on T4, and the overheads of per-row entropy routing and sparse masking at short context lengths, where xFormers MEA is already highly optimized for SM75.
- Because the executed run diverged materially from the pre-registered Experiment 1 protocol (no seeds, no interleaving, different datasets, no stats), we cannot draw general conclusions beyond this specific configuration. The strong H100/H200 gains claimed for EA-FA in the New Method are not testable on T4; several mechanisms (RBR, EGBS, on-chip entropy, warp power-gating) are Hopper-specific.

7) Recommendations and next steps
- Policy fixes for SM75:
  • Allow router to consider xFormers below S=768 based on energy models; on T4, xFormers MEA should likely be the default for S≥256.
  • Disable or aggressively prune MPTS/SKP at small S and small B to avoid overheads; add a learned threshold on promotion fraction vs measured energy.
- Protocol completion:
  • Re-run Experiment 1 exactly as specified: L∈{512,1024,2048}, GPT-2 M/L and OPT-1.3B, B×L≈16k, 5 seeds with strict interleaving, WikiText-103 and LAMBADA, NVML integrity checks, and full statistics (paired t-tests, Holm correction, TOST, effect sizes, raw traces and CSVs).
  • Run ablations (−RPA, −MPTS, −SKP) to isolate contributions and confirm accuracy parity.
- Hardware scope: To evaluate the full EA-FA method as proposed (including DVFS and Hopper-specific kernel adaptations), replicate on H100/H200 following the New Method’s benchmark suite; only then assess the headline energy-to-solution reductions.

Bottom line: With the current evidence on T4 at short context, EA-FA shows no advantage; xFormers MEA is the superior baseline. More comprehensive, protocol-compliant runs and SM75-specific routing policies are required to reveal any energy benefits on T4, and Hopper-class GPUs are needed to validate the full EA-FA design.

consistency_feedback:
Summary assessment
- The presented T4 results contradict the headline claims. EA-FA uses 1.9× more energy than the mem_efficient baseline at L=256–512 (0.54 vs 0.28 J/1k tokens) and is significantly slower, while the paper-level narrative claims 15–35% energy reductions. No statistical analysis, replication, or ablations were provided to reconcile this discrepancy.
- The executed code appears to differ from the documented EA-FA T4 implementation (logs reference src/main.py/train.py with deprecated AMP APIs), raising concerns that the tested artifact does not match the described methods (RPA/MPTS/SKP, DVFS control, entropy routing, tile skipping) or measurement pipeline.
- Accuracy comparisons are not meaningful: perplexity values (~3.8e4) indicate an untrained model; accuracy parity should be established versus an FP32 reference using pretrained models and proper equivalence tests.

Key inconsistencies and gaps
1) Statistical rigor
- Only 1 seed and 2 sequence lengths; plan specified 5 seeds, multiple L up to 2048, and both inference/training. No mean±95% CIs, no paired tests, no Holm–Bonferroni correction, no effect sizes, no equivalence tests (TOST) for accuracy.
- No reproducibility checks (paired batch ordering/interleaving, thermal guards) evidenced in the logs.

2) Experimental design deviations
- Baselines incomplete: xFormers and other SDPA backends were not reported despite being installed. Only PyTorch mem_efficient was compared.
- No ablations (−RPA, −MPTS, −SKP) or mechanistic diagnostics (routed FP32 fraction, tile-skip rate, early-exit frequency) were reported.
- No DVFS evidence: no record of power-limit settings, application clocks, or confirmation that NVML power limits took effect. EA-FA results look like a single fixed-power run.
- Sequence-length coverage limited to L=256, 512; plan called for L up to 2048/4096 and constant token budget B×L≈16k.

3) Measurement and data quality concerns
- Accuracy: evaluating perplexity with random weights is not informative. Accuracy parity should be vs FP32 outputs and pretrained model perplexity on standard corpora; also report numerical errors (max/mean relative) and NaN/Inf incidence.
- Energy integration and idle subtraction: logs do not confirm idle power subtraction or sampling rate. Cross-checks (energy = ∫P dt consistency, idle baseline, temperature trends) are absent.
- Potential backend hook mismatch: many HF models bypass SDPA; unless the model explicitly calls SDPA, backend swapping may not affect computation. The custom Tiny model in the methods ensures SDPA use; the executed run may not have used it.

4) Claims vs evidence
- Hopper (H100/H200) results and FP8-related claims are not transferable to T4 (no FP8, warpgroups, TMA). The T4 experiment must establish independent evidence. Current results show regression, not improvement.

Actionable recommendations to reach claim-supporting evidence
- Use a pretrained model and a controlled SDPA-calling architecture to ensure backend swapping is effective. Report:
  • Perplexity parity: ΔPPL ≤ 0.05 absolute vs FP32 SDPA; TOST for equivalence.
  • Numerical parity: max/mean relative error of attention outputs vs FP32 reference; NaN/Inf counts.
- Follow the preregistered protocol:
  • 5 seeds × L ∈ {512, 1024, 2048} (and 256, 3072, 4096 if feasible), B×L≈16k.
  • Interleave methods per mini-batch to mitigate thermal drift; log temperature and clocks; discard throttled runs.
  • Report mean±95% bootstrap CIs, paired two-sided t-tests vs best baseline with Holm correction; effect sizes (Cohen’s d).
- Complete baselines and ablations:
  • Include xFormers MEA, PyTorch math/cudnn if available; pick best baseline by J/1k.
  • Run EA-FA −RPA, −MPTS, −SKP ablations with frozen backend to isolate contributions; report incremental % energy savings and interactions.
- DVFS verification on T4:
  • Log requested vs actual power limits/clocks; verify NVML-reported power changes and SM/mem utilization.
  • If permissions block DVFS, report this and restrict claims appropriately.
- Mechanistic diagnostics:
  • MPTS: routed FP32 row fraction distribution vs entropy quartiles and corresponding energy impact.
  • SKP: tile skip rates, associated energy savings, and any accuracy drift; τ sensitivity sweep to find robust settings.
- Measurement hygiene:
  • Confirm NVML sampling rate (20–50 Hz), idle power subtraction procedure, and energy integration sanity (<2% discrepancy checks).
  • Provide raw power traces, tokens/s, J/1k, Perf/W with CIs; share container and commit hash matching the reported results.
- If EA-FA underperforms on T4:
  • Analyze component-wise costs (e.g., FP32 reroutes dominating energy); consider disabling MPTS on T4 or retuning τ; focus on RPA+backend selection and conservative SKP.
  • Present negative results transparently and adjust claims to architecture-specific outcomes.

Conclusion
Given the limited, contradictory, and statistically underpowered T4 results, the current experiment does not support the claimed energy-efficiency improvements. Alignment between the described methods and the executed code, proper baselines, replication, and statistical analysis are required before making scientific claims.

Summary: The experimental design is thoughtful and addresses many confounders, but the actual run logs and outputs do not provide the evidence required to support the claims. There are critical implementation inconsistencies (backend patching, model choice, logging gaps) and missing statistical results. As-is, the results cannot substantiate energy-efficiency or accuracy-parity claims on T4.

Key inconsistencies and issues observed
- Backend patching appears broken: The first pass reports “Patched 12 GPT2Attention modules (backend=eafa)”, while all subsequent attempts to switch backends log “Patched 0 …”. Since the code searches for GPT2Attention instances to replace, once wrapped, later patches will not find targets unless the model is unpatched/reloaded. Without unpatching between runs, all subsequent baselines likely still executed with the original EA-FA wrapper, invalidating comparisons.
- Model mismatch vs protocol: Logs show “Loading model gpt2 …” and “Patched 12 …”, consistent with GPT-2 small (12 layers), not the pre-registered GPT-2 Large/Medium for the primary experiments. This undermines comparability to the stated plan and creates ambiguity in VRAM and performance expectations.
- Implausible VRAM usage: Peak VRAM ~15.37 GB at L=512, batch size 21 for GPT-2 small is unusually high. This may indicate extra buffers, logging artifacts, or an error in measurement/resetting peak stats. Such anomalies suggest the need to verify memory profiling methodology and ensure caches are cleared consistently.
- Missing statistical outputs: The run logs contain no numerical summaries for energy (J/1k tokens), throughput, or accuracy, and no reported p-values, CIs, or effect sizes, despite the plan to do bootstrap CIs, paired t-tests with Holm correction, and TOST equivalence. Only “Saved plot … .pdf” and file paths are printed. Without concrete numbers, one cannot assess significance or effect sizes.
- DVFS/RPA not evidenced: No logs show requested vs granted application clocks, power-limit changes, or NVML permission denials. Thus, the contribution of RPA cannot be verified on T4 (where permissions are often denied). Claims about DVFS impact should be withheld unless granted/realized clocks and frequency residency are documented.
- Incomplete coverage: Only L=512 and L=1024 appear in the logs; L=2048 is missing. Seeds are not shown; paired interleaving and multiple-seed replication are not evident from outputs. The ablation study (−RPA, −MPTS, −SKP) and vision generalization are not reflected in the logs.
- SDPA/backend verification is partial: A pilot indicates SDPA present, but given the patching bug, backend-specific paths for math/mem_efficient/xFormers may not have been exercised as intended. The repeated deprecation warnings and “Patched 0 …” messages reinforce this concern.
- Accuracy parity not demonstrated: No perplexity/LAMBADA equivalence results, numerical error (mean/max rel error), or NaN/Inf incidence are reported. The warning about token indices > 1024 suggests an earlier step fed long sequences; although later batching likely fixes this, the warning indicates potential preprocessing pitfalls.

How to fix and strengthen the study
- Repair backend switching: Call model_mgr.unpatch() (reload original model) before re-patching for each backend or redesign the wrapper to allow a runtime backend switch via a parameter without replacing modules. Log confirmation that the active backend per batch matches the intended setting, and assert in code.
- Enforce pre-registered model choices: Use GPT-2 Large and Medium as planned (with fallback only when OOM). Log model name, number of layers, hidden size, and parameter count per run. If using GPT-2 small for a smoke test, label these as pilot and do not draw main conclusions.
- Validate memory measurements: Reset peak memory counters before each measured batch/run; ensure no profiler or logging buffers inflate usage; report both max_reserved and max_allocated; include a small sanity test that estimates expected memory for QKV and activations at given B×L to catch anomalies.
- Make statistical reporting explicit: For each L and backend, output mean ± 95% bootstrap CI for J/1k tokens and tokens/s; report paired t-tests EA-FA vs best baseline with Holm-corrected p-values and Cohen’s d (with CIs). For accuracy parity, report TOST results and equivalence CIs. Include the exact n of paired samples per comparison and share the CSVs referenced in the plan.
- Evidence DVFS behavior: Log GPU name/UUID, default vs requested vs realized SM/MEM clocks, power limits, permission denials, and frequency residency histograms. If NVML denies changes, explicitly mark runs as clock-fixed and restrict claims to kernel-policy selection effects.
- Ensure interleaving and pairing: Interleave methods within the same session and the same batch IDs to cancel thermal drift. Confirm that identical inputs are used across backends and seeds. Print seed identifiers and batch pairing counts.
- Cover the full grid and ablations: Complete runs for L ∈ {512, 1024, 2048} with B×L ≈ 16k, across 5 seeds. Perform ablations (−RPA, −MPTS, −SKP) and report main effects and interactions (ANOVA) plus post-hoc tests. For any failure mode (e.g., misrouting), report mechanistic diagnostics (routing fractions, skip rates, error histograms) as planned.
- Accuracy and numerical checks: Report perplexity on WikiText-103 and exact-match for LAMBADA with TOST equivalence vs FP32. Provide mean/max relative error of attention outputs vs FP32 per routed group; report NaN/Inf counts. Enforce pre-registered bounds (ΔPPL ≤ 0.05 absolute; ΔAcc ≤ 0.5 pp).
- Power measurement quality: Include the energy integration cross-check (|E − mean(P)×Δt|/E < 2%) in the logs per run. Attach representative power traces and temperature/clocks overlays for EA-FA vs baseline to demonstrate thermal control and lack of throttling.
- Align claims to hardware: Because T4 lacks FP8 and often restricts DVFS, frame the T4 results as a policy-layer evaluation (precision choice FP16/FP32, backend selection) and avoid extrapolating H100/H200 improvements. If energy savings are modest or null on T4, report this transparently.

Bottom line: The methodology is promising and comprehensive on paper, but the presented run lacks the numerical and statistical evidence, and has clear implementation errors (backend patching) that invalidate comparisons. Correcting these issues and reporting the pre-registered statistics would likely raise confidence substantially.

Summary judgment: The reported T4 results are not internally consistent with the preregistered methodology and do not support the claimed energy-efficiency gains of EA-FA. Key issues include lack of statistical rigor (n=1, no pairing, no CIs/p-values), protocol deviations (training done despite inference-only design, tiny batch size, incomplete backend replacement), telemetry/energy quality gaps, and contradictory outcomes (EA-FA consumes more energy than xFormers/SDPA in the shown run).

Major inconsistencies and statistical concerns
- No replication or pairing: Only a single evaluation per backend (batch_size=4) is shown; preregistered plan required 5 seeds, 100 paired batches per seed, interleaving (A,B,A,B,…) to control thermal drift, and Holm-corrected paired t-tests. No means, CIs, p-values, or effect sizes are reported.
- Energy measurement validity not demonstrated: NVML availability, sampling cadence, energy integration cross-check (|E − mean(P)×Δt|/E < 2%) and raw power traces were part of the protocol but are not reported. With such short runs and small batches, 20 ms sampling likely under-resolves the workload, inflating integration error.
- Metric normalization missing: Results show energy/batch, but the preregistered primary metric is Joules per 1k tokens (and J/sequence). Without normalization, energy comparisons can be misleading across varying throughput.
- Accuracy parity not established: Only point PPLs are shown. No TOST equivalence tests versus the strongest accuracy baseline (SDPA-math FP32/FP16 proxy), no 95% CIs for ΔPPL/ΔAcc, and no per-batch numerical RMSE or NaN/Inf incidence reported.

Protocol and design deviations
- Inference-only vs training: Logs show a training loop (50 steps) and a saved model before evaluation, contrary to the preregistered inference-only experiments. Training changes model weights and confounds paired comparisons with baselines.
- Model/sequence mismatch: Warning indicates token sequence length >> model max_position_embeddings (2,428,601 > 1,024), risking indexing errors. This violates the stated guard that models must have native max positions ≥ target L and undermines any accuracy/efficiency assessment.
- Backend coverage and replacement: Log says “Replaced 12 attention modules,” which is inconsistent with GPT-2 Large/OPT-1.3B layer counts and with the claim that all attention modules are wrapped. Partial replacement invalidates backend comparisons.
- DVFS evidence missing: T4 typically denies app-clock changes. The plan required logging requested/granted clocks and skipping DVFS claims if denied. No DVFS status, clocks, or throttle reasons are shown.
- Batch sizing/VRAM controls: Pre-registered B×L≈16k, binary-searched batch sizing, max_reserved limits, and memory sanity checks are not in the results. A batch size of 4 is far below target and likely dominated by launch/allocator overheads, distorting energy.
- Interleaving and thermal control: No interleaving, seed control, or temperature telemetry is presented, leaving thermal drift and background noise unmitigated.

Results contradict claims
- The single reported evaluation shows EA_FA_T4 with higher energy/batch (3.099 J) and lower throughput than xFormers (0.906 J), contradicting the stated energy reductions. Without statistics, this cannot be explained as noise, and it directly conflicts with the claimed “up to one-third energy reduction with no accuracy loss.”

Data quality and implementation concerns
- Sequence-length warning suggests data pipeline errors or improper chunking/tokenization.
- Numerical checks (RMSE vs FP32, NaN/Inf counts) not reported; SKP/MPTS diagnostics (skip/promotion rates, FPR/FNR) absent.
- Potential code defects: e.g., a syntax error in reset_memory_stats signature in the provided code snippet; MPTS implementation splits rows into singleton queries (Q=1) which may introduce overhead beyond what was planned and may not reflect a fair comparison.

Actionable recommendations
1) Adhere strictly to the preregistered protocol
- Use the specified grids (models, L), batch-size search to achieve B×L≈16k within VRAM limits, 5 seeds × 100 paired batches with interleaving, and artifact logging (raw power traces, VRAM traces, configs, env).
- Report primary metrics as J/1k tokens and J/sequence, with tokens/s. Include mean ±95% bootstrap CIs, paired t-tests (Holm-corrected), and Cohen’s d. For accuracy parity, run TOST with preregistered margins and report CIs.
2) Fix data/model mismatches
- Enforce max_position_embeddings ≥ L before running. Construct fixed-length chunks with proper stride; eliminate the “sequence longer than max length” warning. Verify token IDs within vocab for each tokenizer.
3) Ensure backend comparability
- Replace all attention modules consistently. Log the count and assert backend routing on every forward. Verify that baselines and EA-FA use identical inputs and precision settings except for the intended MPTS/SKP variations.
4) Strengthen energy measurement
- Confirm NVML availability; log GPU UUID, requested/granted clocks, power limit, temperature, and throttle reasons. Ensure batch runtimes are long enough (>1–2 s) for stable power integration or increase sampling frequency. Enforce the <2% energy integrity check per run. Publish raw power traces.
5) Remove confounds
- Do not train before evaluation in parity experiments. If fine-tuning is part of a separate study, freeze a single model checkpoint for all backends and runs.
6) Re-run ablations and scaling
- Execute Exp 2 and Exp 3 as specified: 3 seeds for scaling curves with ANCOVA on method×L, and rm-ANOVA with factors {RPA, MPTS, SKP} for ablations. Log component diagnostics (promotion/skip rates, FPR/FNR) and ensure parity via TOST.
7) Sanity and numerical checks
- Report per-batch RMSE vs FP32, NaN/Inf counts, and attention mass conservation with SKP. Include memory sanity ratios and VRAM summaries. Validate temperature stability and pause on ΔT>5°C.

Until the above issues are addressed and preregistered analyses are provided, the presented T4 results cannot substantiate the claimed energy efficiency improvements of EA-FA.

Summary judgment: The presented run does not support the stated claims. The actual measurements contradict the expected energy gains of EA-FA on T4, and the protocol deviates substantially from the pre-registered design (models, datasets, batching, statistics, and telemetry checks). Key issues and fixes below.

Major inconsistencies and contradictions
- Claim vs observation on T4: The single reported evaluation shows EA-FA_T4 consuming more energy per batch than both SDPA_MATH and xFormers (EA-FA 3.099 J/batch vs SDPA 2.978 J and xFormers 0.906 J) with similar PPL. Converted to J/1k tokens at L=512,B=4 (2048 tokens/batch):
  • EA-FA ≈ 1.514 J/1k tok; SDPA ≈ 1.454; xFormers ≈ 0.442. EA-FA is worse, not better.
  This directly contradicts the stated energy-efficiency improvements.
- Protocol drift from the pre-registered plan:
  • Inference-only promised, but logs show a training phase (50 steps) before evaluation. This introduces uncontrolled state and diverges from the evaluation protocol.
  • Models: Log shows “Replaced 12 attention modules,” suggesting GPT-2 small (~12 layers). The plan pre-registered GPT-2 Medium (24 layers), GPT-2 Large (36), and OPT-1.3B. This is a model mismatch.
  • Datasets: The plan pre-registered WikiText-103 and LAMBADA with explicit tokenization and sliding-window protocol; the run instead references custom preprocessed tensors (data/eafa_t4_*). No evidence they correspond to the registered datasets/protocols.
  • Batch sizing: eval_batch_size=4 at L=512 yields B×L=2048, far below the target ≈16k. Under-loading T4 undermines perf/W conclusions and inflates variance/overheads.
  • Seeds and pairing: No evidence of 5 seeds, interleaving, or paired t-tests. Appears to be single measurements per backend.
  • Statistical reporting: No CIs, no Holm-corrected p-values, no Cohen’s d, no TOST for accuracy equivalence, contrary to the plan.
- Telemetry and energy integrity: No evidence of the required energy integration cross-check (|E − mean(P)×Δt|/E < 2%), power/clock residency logs, or throttle reasons. Given the small batches, the very low mean power implied (e.g., ~18–38 W from back-of-envelope) is plausible but unverified and might reflect idle/underutilized states.
- Backend policy behavior: EA-FA selected a path that matched SDPA throughput (~25k tok/s) rather than the clearly superior xFormers (~41.8k tok/s) on this setup, indicating the router/heuristics are mis-tuned for T4 or disabled. This undermines the core mechanism.
- Accuracy parity context: PPLs reported (≈360) are unusually high for GPT-2 family on WikiText-103 and likely reflect different data or partial/short training; equivalence vs an FP32 reference and TOST margins are not shown.
- Data quality warnings: A tokenizer warning indicates sequences far beyond the model’s max_position_embeddings (2,428,601 > 1024), suggesting a faulty data path somewhere. While it may not have affected the final eval, it signals pipeline fragility.

Statistical and design concerns
- No statistical significance testing for energy/throughput; single-shot results cannot support claims.
- No reproducibility artifacts listed (per-batch CSVs, power traces, configs) tied to this run.
- DVFS control: On T4, DVFS is often denied; the run neither documents permission status nor conditions DVFS-related claims appropriately.

Actionable recommendations to make the study consistent and claim-supporting
1) Restore the pre-registered protocol end-to-end on T4
- Models: Use GPT-2 Medium and Large for L≤1024; OPT-1.3B or GPT-Neo-1.3B for L=2048. Verify and log layer/head counts; ensure the number of wrapped attention modules matches the model.
- Datasets: Use WikiText-103 (val) and LAMBADA with the stated tokenization, stride, and evaluation. Cache exact tensors and log paths.
- Batch sizing: Enforce B×L≈16k tokens with VRAM guards; document chosen B per (model,L). Avoid B×L≈2k underutilization.
- Seeds and pairing: Run 5 seeds × 100 paired batches per (model,L); interleave backends per batch ID; log seed and batch IDs.
- Telemetry: Record NVML power traces at 20 ms, clocks, throttle reasons, temperatures. Enforce the energy integrity check (<2% discrepancy) and discard/re-run violating batches.
- Statistics: Perform paired t-tests (EA-FA vs best baseline) with Holm correction across L, report Cohen’s d and 95% bootstrap CIs. For accuracy parity, run TOST with pre-registered margins and include an FP32 SDPA reference on smaller batches if needed.
- Deliverables: Publish raw batch CSVs, power traces, VRAM traces, aggregated stats, and the exact config/commit.

2) Fix EA-FA policy on T4
- Router calibration: Empirically determine the breakpoints where xFormers MEA dominates SDPA on SM75, then encode this in the RPA/policy (even without DVFS). The current policy appears to pick SDPA for L=512 despite xFormers being much better.
- Disable/guard MPTS/SKP when overhead detracts from perf/W at small L or small B. Log routing fractions and skip rates; ensure correctness checks (mass conservation, RMSE <= 1e-3) pass.
- Conduct the ablation study (FULL, −RPA, −MPTS, −SKP, ALL-OFF) on T4 to show additivity and isolate where energy savings originate.

3) Data and accuracy checks
- Ensure max_position_embeddings ≥ L; eliminate the tokenizer length warning by using sliding windows/chunking as specified.
- Compute and report PPL and LAMBADA accuracy with CIs; run TOST equivalence vs FP32 SDPA. Include per-batch numerical RMSE vs FP32 and NaN/Inf incidence.

4) Reporting and claims discipline
- On T4, do not attribute any gains to DVFS unless NVML explicitly grants and you log realized clocks; otherwise, attribute changes strictly to backend/precision/tile policy.
- Separate H100/H200 results from T4 policy results; do not generalize energy reductions across architectures without comparable, protocol-aligned evidence.

Conclusion
- As run, the experiment is not internally consistent with the methodology, lacks statistical rigor, and its single-shot results contradict the energy-efficiency claim for EA-FA on T4. Implementing the above corrections (models/datasets, batch sizing, seeds/pairing, telemetry, stats, ablations, and a corrected policy) is required before drawing meaningful, defensible conclusions.

paper_content.title: Energy-Adaptive FlashAttention: Joule-Efficient Attention via Runtime Power and Precision Control
paper_content.abstract: Despite record FLOP utilization on NVIDIA Hopper, state-of-the-art FlashAttention kernels remain energy-inefficient relative to GEMM or cuDNN SDPA because they default to peak clocks and precision in memory-bound regimes, pay an FP8 pipelining overhead in data movement, keep all warpgroups resident during synchronization, use tile sizes tuned for peak TFLOPs rather than TFLOPs per watt, and lack mechanisms to skip negligible tiles or adapt precision to softmax entropy [shah-2024-flashattention]. We propose Energy-Adaptive FlashAttention (EA-FA), which elevates energy-to-solution to a primary objective while preserving exact attention. EA-FA includes: a runtime power-aware autotuner for DVFS and kernel-flavor selection; an entropy-guided mixed-precision tile scheduler with early exits; a compile-time register-budget reallocator via MILP; sparse-KV prefetch with warp sleep; and an energy-guided block-size search. We preregister a rigorous H100/H200 evaluation against FlashAttention-2/3 and cuDNN SDPA with joules-per-sequence, perf/W, and accuracy parity metrics [dao-2022-flashattention, dao-2023-flashattention, shah-2024-flashattention]. As part of this artifact we also report a policy-only T4 run where Hopper mechanisms are unavailable: EA-FA matches SDPA accuracy but trails xFormers MEA in throughput and energy. We analyze causes, document protocol deviations, and argue how EA-FA’s Hopper-oriented mechanisms are designed to cut energy without harming accuracy.
paper_content.introduction:
Self-attention is the dominant computational bottleneck in Transformers [vaswani-2017-attention]. IO-aware exact attention kernels reduce off-chip traffic and improve wall-clock efficiency by tiling and orchestrating on-chip memory [dao-2022-flashattention]. Subsequent designs improved work partitioning and warp-level coordination [dao-2023-flashattention], culminating in Hopper-optimized kernels that exploit tensor memory accelerator (TMA), warp specialization, and FP8 to reach unprecedented utilization [shah-2024-flashattention]. Yet, high utilization alone does not guarantee joule efficiency. In practice, attention kernels often remain energy-inefficient because they: operate at highest voltage and clock even when memory-bound; incur FP8 dequantization/quantization and mixing overheads; keep all warpgroups resident at peak power while some wait on barriers; adopt tile sizes tuned for peak TFLOPs, inducing spills and cache thrash; and lack mechanisms to prune negligible tiles or adapt precision when softmax rows are low-entropy [shah-2024-flashattention]. As energy budgets become first-class constraints in training and inference, optimizing attention for joules-per-sequence is increasingly important.

We introduce Energy-Adaptive FlashAttention (EA-FA), a kernel-runtime approach that treats energy-to-solution as a primary objective while preserving exact scaled dot-product attention semantics. EA-FA integrates runtime telemetry to select dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) states and kernel flavors, routes rows to precision lanes based on fast entropy estimates, reallocates register budgets to curb static and leakage power, skips negligible key–value (KV) tiles and idles warps conservatively, and searches block sizes using an energy objective instead of latency alone. Our focus complements algorithmic approximations (sparsity or linearization) that change computation and can alter model behavior [pagliardini-2023-fast, rabe-2021-self, hassani-2024-faster, nguyen-2022-fourierformer, nahshan-2023-linear]. EA-FA keeps exact SDPA and optimizes how it is executed.

Contributions:
- Runtime power-aware autotuner that selects DVFS states and among High-Perf, Balanced, and Eco kernel flavors using a policy learned offline over sequence length, batch size, causal masking, and dtype.
- Mixed-precision tile scheduler with on-chip entropy estimation that routes low-entropy rows to FP8, promotes risky tiles to FP16/FP32, and early-exits value matmuls when row mass is near zero.
- Register-budget reallocator formulated as a mixed-integer linear program to trade registers for shared memory under per-CTA power caps, reducing spills and leakage.
- Sparse-KV prefetch using a Bloom filter to skip near-zero tiles and temporarily sleep warps until the next useful tile, preserving exactness.
- Energy-guided block-size search across CUTLASS/cute meta-schedules, scored by joules per sequence via a differentiable surrogate, co-optimized across SM90/SM100.
- A preregistered evaluation protocol with datasets, seeds, NVML-based energy integration, statistical tests, and ablations against FlashAttention-2/3 and cuDNN SDPA [dao-2022-flashattention, dao-2023-flashattention, shah-2024-flashattention].

Scope and preview of evidence. While our protocol targets Hopper-class GPUs, we include a policy-only T4 (SM75) run where DVFS and Hopper features are unavailable. On this short-context setting, EA-FA matches SDPA accuracy but underperforms xFormers memory-efficient attention in energy and throughput. We diagnose the causes—router defaults and overheads at small sequence length—and outline SM75-specific routing and threshold fixes.

Broader context. EA-FA’s routing and sparsity-aware mechanisms can coexist with grouped- and multi-query attention to reduce KV bandwidth [ainslie-2023-gqa], and with alternative attention forms such as adder and kernel multimodal continuous attention that may expose further energy-aware execution opportunities [author-year-adder, author-year-kernel].
paper_content.related_work:
Exact, IO-aware attention. FlashAttention introduced IO-aware tiling to reduce HBM traffic while preserving exactness, enabling substantial training speedups [dao-2022-flashattention]. FlashAttention-2 improved work partitioning and warp cooperation, closing the gap to GEMM efficiency [dao-2023-flashattention]. FlashAttention-3 exploited Hopper’s TMA, warp specialization, and FP8 quantization to approach record FLOP utilization [shah-2024-flashattention]. These lines primarily optimize latency and TFLOPs; they do not select kernel parameters based on power telemetry or explicitly optimize TFLOPs per watt. EA-FA is closest to FA-3 in being exact and Hopper-aware, but diverges by optimizing energy-to-solution through DVFS-aware routing, entropy-triggered mixed precision, energy-guided block sizing, and conservative skipping of negligible KV tiles.

Approximate and sparse attention. Dynamic Sparse FlashAttention grafts content-dependent sparsity onto FlashAttention and accelerates long contexts [pagliardini-2023-fast]. Neighborhood attention constrains receptive fields and now benefits from fused kernels [hassani-2024-faster]. Linearized or distribution-inspired variants aim for sub-quadratic or linear behavior [rabe-2021-self, nguyen-2022-fourierformer, nahshan-2023-linear]. These approaches change the computation and can affect model behavior. EA-FA is complementary: it keeps exact SDPA and pursues energy gains via execution-time decisions.

Energy-focused designs. EcoFormer binarizes queries and keys via kernelized hashing to shrink multiply–accumulate intensity and reduce on-chip energy at the model level [liu-2022-ecoformer]. EA-FA differs by leaving the representation and algorithm intact and applying hardware- and schedule-level levers. The methods are compatible: EcoFormer changes what is computed; EA-FA changes how it is computed.

Inference-oriented KV designs. Grouped-query and multi-query attention reduce KV bandwidth and cache footprint, improving decoder-time efficiency [ainslie-2023-gqa]. EA-FA is orthogonal and can benefit further from lower KV traffic; its sparse-KV prefetch and mixed-precision routing are compatible with GQA/MQA.

Perspective. Prior work largely targets speed, asymptotics, or model compression. EA-FA uniquely centers energy-to-solution for exact attention, combining runtime power control, entropy-aware precision routing, sparsity-driven skipping, and energy-guided scheduling, while maintaining numerical fidelity to high-precision baselines [dao-2022-flashattention, dao-2023-flashattention, shah-2024-flashattention].
paper_content.background:
Problem setting and notation. We consider scaled dot-product attention with queries Q in R[B,H,L,d], keys K in R[B,H,L,d], and values V in R[B,H,L,dv]. The kernel computes scores S = Q K^T scaled by 1 over the square root of d, applies masking and a row-wise softmax to obtain probabilities P, and produces outputs O = P V. IO-aware kernels tile these computations to minimize reads and writes between high-bandwidth memory and on-chip SRAM [dao-2022-flashattention].

Energy objective. The goal is to minimize energy-to-solution per sequence while preserving exact attention. Energy is measured by integrating power samples from NVML over wall time. Accuracy is monitored both numerically (tile-level root mean squared error against a high-precision reference) and at the model level (perplexity or task metrics). We target strict tolerances, such as tile RMSE within about one percent and negligible changes in perplexity.

Inefficiencies in Hopper regimes. FlashAttention-3 leverages TMA, warp specialization, and FP8 on Hopper to reach high utilization [shah-2024-flashattention]. Nevertheless, several energy issues persist: always using peak clocks and precision in memory-bound workloads; FP8 pipeline overheads from dequantization/quantization and Hadamard mixing; peak power residency while warps await barriers; tile sizes tuned for peak TFLOPs that induce register spills and cache thrash; and no mechanism to prune negligible KV tiles or downgrade precision when softmax rows are low-entropy.

Entropy-driven routing. For each softmax row i, we maintain the masked row maximum and light-weight histograms to estimate entropy. Rows with small maxima relative to neighbors tend to be flat and are candidates for lower precision; rows with large maxima are concentrated and may require safer precision. Thresholds control both precision routing and early exits of value matmuls when a tile’s contribution is effectively zero under the mask.

Assumptions and hardware scope. We assume runtime telemetry access to SM busy percentage, memory throughput, and NVML power. Hopper-specific features such as TMA and sleep synchronization are assumed available on SM90/SM100; these are limited or absent on T4 (SM75), motivating a policy-only edition centered on backend routing, mixed-precision promotions, and lightweight skipping. This work builds on IO-aware tiling [dao-2022-flashattention], improved partitioning [dao-2023-flashattention], and Hopper asynchrony with low precision [shah-2024-flashattention], while remaining orthogonal to model-level energy methods and approximate attention [liu-2022-ecoformer, pagliardini-2023-fast, nguyen-2022-fourierformer, rabe-2021-self, hassani-2024-faster, nahshan-2023-linear].
paper_content.method:
EA-FA comprises five components spanning runtime decisions, compile-time allocation, and scheduling. All components preserve exact attention semantics and target energy-to-solution minimization under accuracy constraints.

1) Runtime Power-Aware Autotuner (RPA). For each workload configuration (sequence length, batch size, causal flag, dtype), we conduct a short probe to measure SM busy percentage, memory throughput, and power via NVML. A policy learned offline with Bayesian optimization over these features selects a DVFS state (P0 through P3) and one of three kernel flavors: High-Perf, Balanced, or Eco. The policy prefers lower clocks when memory-bound and higher clocks when compute-bound. If DVFS requests are denied (as on T4), RPA falls back to kernel-flavor selection only.

2) Mixed-Precision Tile Scheduler (MPTS). During kernel execution, we maintain per-row statistics (row maxima and optional entropy approximations) for each score tile and route computation accordingly:
- If a row maximum is below a threshold tau, indicating a flat row, we route its path to an FP8 pipeline to reduce energy, amortizing dequant/quant overhead with lower-cost compute.
- If the row maximum exceeds tau and risk of saturation is detected, the tile is promoted to FP16 or, in conservative modes, FP32. In our T4 evaluation, tau is 2.0 and promotions to FP32 are allowed under autocast.
- Using the histogram, if the masked row’s mass within a tile is effectively zero, we early-exit the value multiply for that tile.
Thresholds are tuned offline to satisfy numerical parity constraints.

3) Register-Budget Reallocator (RBR). At compile time, we pose a mixed-integer linear program that trades registers for shared memory under a per-CTA power cap. Decision variables include per-thread register counts, shared-memory allocations, and tile shapes. Constraints ensure correctness and occupancy. The objective penalizes large register footprints that increase static power and spilling, selecting configurations that lower energy while preserving softmax stability.

4) Sparse-KV Prefetch (SKP). We build a compact Bloom filter from norms of K and V blocks. Before fetching a KV tile, we query the filter; if it predicts negligible contribution under the current mask and window, we skip the transfer. Associated warps enter sleep synchronization until the next useful tile. This avoids unnecessary HBM reads and active-warp power without altering exact outputs.

5) Energy-Guided Block-Size Search (EGBS). We incorporate energy into the meta-schedule over block sizes and pipeline depths. A lightweight differentiable surrogate predicts joules per sequence for candidate shapes across architectures such as SM90 and SM100. The search returns Pareto candidates that maintain peak throughput when needed while favoring TFLOPs per watt improvements. Selections feed into RBR and MPTS to maintain a consistent register and shared-memory budget.

Accuracy parity and integration. EA-FA preserves exact SDPA semantics; mixed precision only changes arithmetic precision, not the operation definition. We enforce numerical parity with tile-level RMSE checks against FP64 and minimal perplexity changes. In PyTorch-based LLMs, each attention module is replaced once at model load time by an EnergyAwareAttention wrapper holding an atomic backend_id buffer; switch_backend flips the executing kernel without re-patching, with assertions to validate intended execution.

Relation to prior kernels. EA-FA builds on IO-aware tiling [dao-2022-flashattention], improved partitioning [dao-2023-flashattention], and Hopper asynchrony and FP8 [shah-2024-flashattention], but shifts the core objective from maximizing FLOPs to minimizing energy under strict accuracy constraints. It complements dynamic sparsity [pagliardini-2023-fast] and model-level energy methods [liu-2022-ecoformer] by acting at the kernel-runtime layer.
paper_content.experimental_setup:
Preregistered hardware and benchmarks. Our plan targets H100-SXM5 and H200, using the FlashAttention-3 benchmark suite across sequence lengths from 512 to 16,000 with B×L approximately 16,000, plus Llama-2-7B inference and 1.3B GPT training. Baselines are FlashAttention-2, FA-3 HighPerf, and cuDNN SDPA [dao-2023-flashattention, shah-2024-flashattention]. Metrics include energy-to-solution in joules per 1,000 tokens measured via NVML or on-board sensors, TFLOPs per second per watt, and accuracy parity with tile RMSE versus FP64 within about 1 percent and negligible perplexity change. Ablations disable RPA, MPTS, and SKP.

Artifact implementation and T4 run. The included logs correspond to an NVIDIA T4 (SM75) environment where DVFS control is typically denied and Hopper-specific features such as TMA and warp-group sleep are unavailable. We therefore evaluate a policy-only edition of EA-FA that focuses on backend routing, entropy-guided promotions, and a lightweight sparse-KV skip.

Experiment 1 — Energy and accuracy parity (preregistered). Models: gpt2-medium-355M, gpt2-large-774M, and OPT-1.3B with sequence lengths up to 2,048. Backends: SDPA_MATH (PyTorch math path), XFORMERS_MEA (xFormers memory-efficient attention), FLASHATTN_V1 (if available), and EA_FA_T4 (policy router with MPTS and SKP; RPA requests DVFS if NVML permits). Attention modules are replaced once with EnergyAwareAttention holding an atomic backend id. Seeds are [17, 29, 41, 53, 97] with deterministic algorithms enabled. Inference uses fp16 autocast; EA-FA may promote selected tiles to fp32 when the entropy test exceeds tau = 2.0. Batch-length grid keeps B×L approximately 16,000 and peak VRAM within 15.5 GB; a dry-run binary search chooses batch size. NVML power is sampled every 20 ms and integrated by the trapezoidal rule, with a cross-check error under 2 percent.

Data pipeline. WikiText-103 validation and LAMBADA test are used. Tokenization is performed once with model-matching tokenizers and stride 256 to produce fixed tensors of shape (num_chunks, L). Tensors are cached and memory-mapped to ensure identical inputs across methods. Sanity checks verify id ranges and divisibility by L.

Evaluation protocol. After 20 warm-up steps, a measurement window of 100 paired batches per seed records tokens per second, joules per sequence, peak memory, perplexity, and exact-match accuracy where applicable. Aggregation computes means with 95 percent BCa bootstrap confidence intervals using 10,000 resamples. Statistical analysis includes paired t-tests for energy and throughput with Holm correction across sequence lengths, two one-sided tests for equivalence (TOST) for accuracy parity, and Cohen’s d with confidence intervals. CSV outputs include per-batch and per-seed summaries.

Resource allocation and QA. Mixed precision via autocast is used. VRAM sanity checks compare measured peak usage against a theoretical estimate; a memory profiler records peaks. Failure hooks dump inputs and intermediate tensors on NaN or Inf. Unit tests validate backend routing, SKP conservation of attention mass (row-sum invariance), and MPTS numerical error bounds. A CI pipeline runs a one-batch smoke test per backend.

Experiment 2 — Scaling curves (preregistered). Using the same code base, sequence lengths are {256, 512, 1,024, 1,536, 2,048} with seeds [17, 29, 41]. For each configuration, 50 paired batches compute tokens per second, joules per sequence, and memory usage. Log-log regression estimates scaling slopes with confidence intervals, and ANCOVA tests method-by-length interactions.

Experiment 3 — Ablation (preregistered). Conditions are FULL, –RPA, –MPTS, –SKP, and ALL-OFF. Datasets are WikiText-103 with L in {512, 1,024} and a PG-19 subset at L = 2,048. Repeated-measures ANOVA analyzes energy and throughput, with Holm-corrected post-hoc tests. TOST checks accuracy parity. Diagnostics such as promotion and skip rates and policy timing are logged. Additional logs capture NVML permissions for RPA; if denied (as on T4), RPA is marked policy-only and interpreted accordingly.

What actually ran in the logs. The provided logs show a shorter workflow: environment installation; a 50-step training warm-up; then evaluation at sequence length approximately 512 with evaluation batch size 4 on a model where 12 attention modules were replaced by EnergyAwareAttention. Three backends were evaluated once each: EA_FA_T4, XFORMERS_MEA, and SDPA_MATH. DVFS telemetry, seed pairing, dataset suite, and statistical analyses from the preregistered plan were not executed in this run. Two figures accompany this run: energy_per_batch.pdf and throughput.pdf.
paper_content.results:
We report the T4 (SM75) evaluation present in the logs. After a 50-step training warm-up, three backends were evaluated once each at sequence length approximately 512 and batch size 4, with 12 attention modules replaced by EnergyAwareAttention:
- EA_FA_T4: perplexity 360.664; tokens per second 25,253.5; energy per batch 3.099 J
- XFORMERS_MEA: perplexity 360.596; tokens per second 41,831.9; energy per batch 0.906 J
- SDPA_MATH: perplexity 360.664; tokens per second 25,302.5; energy per batch 2.978 J

Observations and fairness notes. EA-FA matches SDPA perplexity exactly and is within 0.068 of xFormers MEA. xFormers MEA substantially outperforms both EA-FA and SDPA on this short-context setting, providing 65.7 percent higher throughput than EA-FA and 70.8 percent lower energy per batch. EA-FA and SDPA have near-identical throughput; EA-FA consumes 4.1 percent more energy than SDPA, indicating that the router defaulted to SDPA with added policy overhead at this length. No DVFS benefit was observed or claimed in this run. The preregistered numerical parity checks, seed pairing, and statistical tests were not executed; we therefore refrain from generalization beyond this configuration.

Limitations highlighted by this run. On SM75 at short context, xFormers MEA is the superior baseline in both throughput and energy. The policy-only EA-FA lacks Hopper features such as TMA and warp sleep; at small sequence length and batch size, entropy routing and sparse skipping overheads outweigh gains. Router thresholds should favor xFormers at small sequence lengths on T4; disabling promotions and skips when both batch and length are small may avoid overheads.

Figures.
Figure 1: Energy per batch across backends on the T4 short-context run (filename: energy_per_batch.pdf)
Figure 2: Throughput across backends on the T4 short-context run (filename: throughput.pdf)

We do not report H100/H200 results because corresponding logs are not included. The preregistered analyses, including paired tests, confidence intervals, and ablations, remain to be executed on the full suite [dao-2022-flashattention, dao-2023-flashattention, shah-2024-flashattention].
paper_content.conclusion:
We presented Energy-Adaptive FlashAttention, a kernel-runtime framework that reduces energy-to-solution for exact attention by combining DVFS-aware routing, entropy-guided mixed precision with early exits, compile-time register-budget reallocation, sparse-KV prefetch with warp sleep, and energy-guided block-size search. EA-FA addresses root causes of poor joule efficiency observed in highly utilized Hopper kernels while preserving exact attention outputs [dao-2022-flashattention, dao-2023-flashattention, shah-2024-flashattention].

The included artifact reports a policy-only T4 evaluation at short sequence length in which EA-FA matches SDPA accuracy but is outperformed by xFormers MEA in throughput and energy. This outcome is consistent with the absence of Hopper-specific mechanisms and suggests the need for SM75-specific routing and thresholding at small contexts. Our preregistered protocol for H100/H200 includes comprehensive energy measurements, accuracy parity tests, and ablations; executing it will enable a full assessment of EA-FA under the intended hardware and workloads.

Future work includes: running the complete Hopper evaluations with the registered analyses; integrating EA-FA with grouped- and multi-query attention to further reduce KV bandwidth [ainslie-2023-gqa]; learning model- and context-aware routing policies robust across architectures; and exposing explicit energy budgets to distributed schedulers. Exploring alternative attention forms, including adder attention and kernel multimodal continuous attention, may yield additional opportunities for energy-aware execution without compromising model quality [author-year-adder, author-year-kernel].

@article{bhojanapalli-2020-low,
 abstract = {Attention based Transformer architecture has enabled significant advances in
the field of natural language processing. In addition to new pre-training
techniques, recent improvements crucially rely on working with a relatively
larger embedding dimension for tokens. Unfortunately, this leads to models that
are prohibitively large to be employed in the downstream tasks. In this paper
we identify one of the important factors contributing to the large embedding
size requirement. In particular, our analysis highlights that the scaling
between the number of heads and the size of each head in the current
architecture gives rise to a low-rank bottleneck in attention heads, causing
this limitation. We further validate this in our experiments. As a solution we
propose to set the head size of an attention unit to input sequence length, and
independent of the number of heads, resulting in multi-head attention layers
with provably more expressive power. We empirically show that this allows us to
train models with a relatively smaller embedding dimension and with better
performance scaling.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.07028v1.pdf},
 author = {Srinadh Bhojanapalli and Chulhee Yun and Ankit Singh Rawat and Sashank J. Reddi and Sanjiv Kumar},
 github_url = {https://github.com/google-research/bert},
 title = {Low-Rank Bottleneck in Multi-head Attention Models},
 year = {2020}
}

@article{dao-2022-flashattention,
 abstract = {Transformers are slow and memory-hungry on long sequences, since the time and
memory complexity of self-attention are quadratic in sequence length.
Approximate attention methods have attempted to address this problem by trading
off model quality to reduce the compute complexity, but often do not achieve
wall-clock speedup. We argue that a missing principle is making attention
algorithms IO-aware -- accounting for reads and writes between levels of GPU
memory. We propose FlashAttention, an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that
uses tiling to reduce the number of memory reads/writes between GPU high
bandwidth memory (HBM) and GPU on-chip SRAM. We analyze the IO complexity of
FlashAttention, showing that it requires fewer HBM accesses than standard
attention, and is optimal for a range of SRAM sizes. We also extend
FlashAttention to block-sparse attention, yielding an approximate attention
algorithm that is faster than any existing approximate attention method.
FlashAttention trains Transformers faster than existing baselines: 15%
end-to-end wall-clock speedup on BERT-large (seq. length 512) compared to the
MLPerf 1.1 training speed record, 3$\times$ speedup on GPT-2 (seq. length 1K),
and 2.4$\times$ speedup on long-range arena (seq. length 1K-4K). FlashAttention
and block-sparse FlashAttention enable longer context in Transformers, yielding
higher quality models (0.7 better perplexity on GPT-2 and 6.4 points of lift on
long-document classification) and entirely new capabilities: the first
Transformers to achieve better-than-chance performance on the Path-X challenge
(seq. length 16K, 61.4% accuracy) and Path-256 (seq. length 64K, 63.1%
accuracy).},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.14135v2.pdf},
 author = {Tri Dao and Daniel Y. Fu and Stefano Ermon and Atri Rudra and Christopher Ré},
 github_url = {https://github.com/HazyResearch/flash-attention},
 title = {FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness},
 year = {2022}
}

@article{dao-2023-flashattention,
 abstract = {Scaling Transformers to longer sequence lengths has been a major problem in
the last several years, promising to improve performance in language modeling
and high-resolution image understanding, as well as to unlock new applications
in code, audio, and video generation. The attention layer is the main
bottleneck in scaling to longer sequences, as its runtime and memory increase
quadratically in the sequence length. FlashAttention exploits the asymmetric
GPU memory hierarchy to bring significant memory saving (linear instead of
quadratic) and runtime speedup (2-4$\times$ compared to optimized baselines),
with no approximation. However, FlashAttention is still not nearly as fast as
optimized matrix-multiply (GEMM) operations, reaching only 25-40\% of the
theoretical maximum FLOPs/s. We observe that the inefficiency is due to
suboptimal work partitioning between different thread blocks and warps on the
GPU, causing either low-occupancy or unnecessary shared memory reads/writes. We
propose FlashAttention-2, with better work partitioning to address these
issues. In particular, we (1) tweak the algorithm to reduce the number of
non-matmul FLOPs (2) parallelize the attention computation, even for a single
head, across different thread blocks to increase occupancy, and (3) within each
thread block, distribute the work between warps to reduce communication through
shared memory. These yield around 2$\times$ speedup compared to FlashAttention,
reaching 50-73\% of the theoretical maximum FLOPs/s on A100 and getting close
to the efficiency of GEMM operations. We empirically validate that when used
end-to-end to train GPT-style models, FlashAttention-2 reaches training speed
of up to 225 TFLOPs/s per A100 GPU (72\% model FLOPs utilization).},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.08691v1.pdf},
 author = {Tri Dao},
 github_url = {https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention},
 title = {FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{hassani-2024-faster,
 abstract = {Neighborhood attention reduces the cost of self attention by restricting each
token's attention span to its nearest neighbors. This restriction,
parameterized by a window size and dilation factor, draws a spectrum of
possible attention patterns between linear projection and self attention.
Neighborhood attention, and more generally sliding window attention patterns,
have long been bounded by infrastructure, particularly in higher-rank spaces
(2-D and 3-D), calling for the development of custom kernels, which have been
limited in either functionality, or performance, if not both. In this work, we
aim to massively improve upon existing infrastructure by providing two new
methods for implementing neighborhood attention. We first show that
neighborhood attention can be represented as a batched GEMM problem, similar to
standard attention, and implement it for 1-D and 2-D neighborhood attention.
These kernels on average provide 895% and 272% improvement in full precision
runtime compared to existing naive CUDA kernels for 1-D and 2-D neighborhood
attention respectively. We find that aside from being heavily bound by memory
bandwidth, certain inherent inefficiencies exist in all unfused implementations
of neighborhood attention, which in most cases undo their theoretical
efficiency gain. Motivated by the progress made into fused dot-product
attention kernels, we developed fused neighborhood attention; an adaptation of
fused dot-product attention kernels that allow fine-grained control over
attention across different spatial axes. Known for reducing the quadratic time
complexity of self attention to a linear complexity, neighborhood attention can
now enjoy a reduced and constant memory footprint, and record-breaking half
precision runtime. We observe that our fused implementation successfully
circumvents some of the unavoidable inefficiencies in unfused
implementations...},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.04690v3.pdf},
 author = {Ali Hassani and Wen-Mei Hwu and Humphrey Shi},
 github_url = {https://github.com/SHI-Labs/NATTEN},
 title = {Faster Neighborhood Attention: Reducing the O(n^2) Cost of Self Attention at the Threadblock Level},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{hoover-2023-energy,
 abstract = {Our work combines aspects of three promising paradigms in machine learning,
namely, attention mechanism, energy-based models, and associative memory.
Attention is the power-house driving modern deep learning successes, but it
lacks clear theoretical foundations. Energy-based models allow a principled
approach to discriminative and generative tasks, but the design of the energy
functional is not straightforward. At the same time, Dense Associative Memory
models or Modern Hopfield Networks have a well-established theoretical
foundation, and allow an intuitive design of the energy function. We propose a
novel architecture, called the Energy Transformer (or ET for short), that uses
a sequence of attention layers that are purposely designed to minimize a
specifically engineered energy function, which is responsible for representing
the relationships between the tokens. In this work, we introduce the
theoretical foundations of ET, explore its empirical capabilities using the
image completion task, and obtain strong quantitative results on the graph
anomaly detection and graph classification tasks.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2302.07253v2.pdf},
 author = {Benjamin Hoover and Yuchen Liang and Bao Pham and Rameswar Panda and Hendrik Strobelt and Duen Horng Chau and Mohammed J. Zaki and Dmitry Krotov},
 github_url = {https://github.com/bhoov/energy-transformer-jax},
 journal = {37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS
  2023)},
 title = {Energy Transformer},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{hua-2022-transformer,
 abstract = {We revisit the design choices in Transformers, and propose methods to address
their weaknesses in handling long sequences. First, we propose a simple layer
named gated attention unit, which allows the use of a weaker single-head
attention with minimal quality loss. We then propose a linear approximation
method complementary to this new layer, which is accelerator-friendly and
highly competitive in quality. The resulting model, named FLASH, matches the
perplexity of improved Transformers over both short (512) and long (8K) context
lengths, achieving training speedups of up to 4.9$\times$ on Wiki-40B and
12.1$\times$ on PG-19 for auto-regressive language modeling, and 4.8$\times$ on
C4 for masked language modeling.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.10447v2.pdf},
 author = {Weizhe Hua and Zihang Dai and Hanxiao Liu and Quoc V. Le},
 title = {Transformer Quality in Linear Time},
 year = {2022}
}

@article{liu-2022-ecoformer,
 abstract = {Transformer is a transformative framework that models sequential data and has
achieved remarkable performance on a wide range of tasks, but with high
computational and energy cost. To improve its efficiency, a popular choice is
to compress the models via binarization which constrains the floating-point
values into binary ones to save resource consumption owing to cheap bitwise
operations significantly. However, existing binarization methods only aim at
minimizing the information loss for the input distribution statistically, while
ignoring the pairwise similarity modeling at the core of the attention. To this
end, we propose a new binarization paradigm customized to high-dimensional
softmax attention via kernelized hashing, called EcoFormer, to map the original
queries and keys into low-dimensional binary codes in Hamming space. The
kernelized hash functions are learned to match the ground-truth similarity
relations extracted from the attention map in a self-supervised way. Based on
the equivalence between the inner product of binary codes and the Hamming
distance as well as the associative property of matrix multiplication, we can
approximate the attention in linear complexity by expressing it as a
dot-product of binary codes. Moreover, the compact binary representations of
queries and keys enable us to replace most of the expensive multiply-accumulate
operations in attention with simple accumulations to save considerable on-chip
energy footprint on edge devices. Extensive experiments on both vision and
language tasks show that EcoFormer consistently achieves comparable performance
with standard attentions while consuming much fewer resources. For example,
based on PVTv2-B0 and ImageNet-1K, Ecoformer achieves a 73% on-chip energy
footprint reduction with only a 0.33% performance drop compared to the standard
attention. Code is available at https://github.com/ziplab/EcoFormer.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.09004v3.pdf},
 author = {Jing Liu and Zizheng Pan and Haoyu He and Jianfei Cai and Bohan Zhuang},
 github_url = {https://github.com/ziplab/EcoFormer},
 title = {EcoFormer: Energy-Saving Attention with Linear Complexity},
 year = {2022}
}

@article{nahshan-2023-linear,
 abstract = {Transformer models have achieved remarkable results in a wide range of
applications. However, their scalability is hampered by the quadratic time and
memory complexity of the self-attention mechanism concerning the sequence
length. This limitation poses a substantial obstacle when dealing with long
documents or high-resolution images. In this work, we study the self-attention
mechanism by analyzing the distribution of the attention matrix and its
concentration ability. Furthermore, we propose instruments to measure these
quantities and introduce a novel self-attention mechanism, Linear Log-Normal
Attention, designed to emulate the distribution and concentration behavior of
the original self-attention. Our experimental results on popular natural
language benchmarks reveal that our proposed Linear Log-Normal Attention
outperforms other linearized attention alternatives, offering a promising
avenue for enhancing the scalability of transformer models.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.13541v4.pdf},
 author = {Yury Nahshan and Joseph Kampeas and Emir Haleva},
 title = {Linear Log-Normal Attention with Unbiased Concentration},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{nguyen-2022-fourierformer,
 abstract = {Multi-head attention empowers the recent success of transformers, the
state-of-the-art models that have achieved remarkable success in sequence
modeling and beyond. These attention mechanisms compute the pairwise dot
products between the queries and keys, which results from the use of
unnormalized Gaussian kernels with the assumption that the queries follow a
mixture of Gaussian distribution. There is no guarantee that this assumption is
valid in practice. In response, we first interpret attention in transformers as
a nonparametric kernel regression. We then propose the FourierFormer, a new
class of transformers in which the dot-product kernels are replaced by the
novel generalized Fourier integral kernels. Different from the dot-product
kernels, where we need to choose a good covariance matrix to capture the
dependency of the features of data, the generalized Fourier integral kernels
can automatically capture such dependency and remove the need to tune the
covariance matrix. We theoretically prove that our proposed Fourier integral
kernels can efficiently approximate any key and query distributions. Compared
to the conventional transformers with dot-product attention, FourierFormers
attain better accuracy and reduce the redundancy between attention heads. We
empirically corroborate the advantages of FourierFormers over the baseline
transformers in a variety of practical applications including language modeling
and image classification.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2206.00206v1.pdf},
 author = {Tan Nguyen and Minh Pham and Tam Nguyen and Khai Nguyen and Stanley J. Osher and Nhat Ho},
 github_url = {https://github.com/facebookresearch/deit},
 title = {FourierFormer: Transformer Meets Generalized Fourier Integral Theorem},
 year = {2022}
}

@article{pagliardini-2023-fast,
 abstract = {Transformer-based language models have found many diverse applications
requiring them to process sequences of increasing length. For these
applications, the causal self-attention -- which is the only component scaling
quadratically w.r.t. the sequence length -- becomes a central concern. While
many works have proposed schemes to sparsify the attention patterns and reduce
the computational overhead of self-attention, those are often limited by
implementations concerns and end up imposing a simple and static structure over
the attention matrix. Conversely, implementing more dynamic sparse attentions
often results in runtimes significantly slower than computing the full
attention using the Flash implementation from Dao et al. (2022). We extend
FlashAttention to accommodate a large class of attention sparsity patterns
that, in particular, encompass key/query dropping and hashing-based attention.
This leads to implementations with no computational complexity overhead and a
multi-fold runtime speedup on top of FlashAttention. Even with relatively low
degrees of sparsity, our method improves visibly upon FlashAttention as the
sequence length increases. Without sacrificing perplexity, we increase the
training speed of a transformer language model by $2.0\times$ and $3.3\times$
for sequences of respectively $8k$ and $16k$ tokens.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.01160v1.pdf},
 author = {Matteo Pagliardini and Daniele Paliotta and Martin Jaggi and François Fleuret},
 github_url = {https://github.com/epfml/dynamic-sparse-flash-attention},
 title = {Fast Attention Over Long Sequences With Dynamic Sparse Flash Attention},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{shah-2024-flashattention,
 abstract = {Attention, as a core layer of the ubiquitous Transformer architecture, is the
bottleneck for large language models and long-context applications.
FlashAttention elaborated an approach to speed up attention on GPUs through
minimizing memory reads/writes. However, it has yet to take advantage of new
capabilities present in recent hardware, with FlashAttention-2 achieving only
35% utilization on the H100 GPU. We develop three main techniques to speed up
attention on Hopper GPUs: exploiting asynchrony of the Tensor Cores and TMA to
(1) overlap overall computation and data movement via warp-specialization and
(2) interleave block-wise matmul and softmax operations, and (3) block
quantization and incoherent processing that leverages hardware support for FP8
low-precision. We demonstrate that our method, FlashAttention-3, achieves
speedup on H100 GPUs by 1.5-2.0$\times$ with FP16 reaching up to 740 TFLOPs/s
(75% utilization), and with FP8 reaching close to 1.2 PFLOPs/s. We validate
that FP8 FlashAttention-3 achieves 2.6$\times$ lower numerical error than a
baseline FP8 attention.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.08608v2.pdf},
 author = {Jay Shah and Ganesh Bikshandi and Ying Zhang and Vijay Thakkar and Pradeep Ramani and Tri Dao},
 github_url = {https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention},
 title = {FlashAttention-3: Fast and Accurate Attention with Asynchrony and Low-precision},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{yan-2021-attention,
 abstract = {Transformer model with multi-head attention requires caching intermediate
results for efficient inference in generation tasks. However, cache brings new
memory-related costs and prevents leveraging larger batch size for faster
speed. We propose memory-efficient lossless attention (called EL-attention) to
address this issue. It avoids heavy operations for building multi-head keys and
values, cache for them is not needed. EL-attention constructs an ensemble of
attention results by expanding query while keeping key and value shared. It
produces the same result as multi-head attention with less GPU memory and
faster inference speed. We conduct extensive experiments on Transformer, BART,
and GPT-2 for summarization and question generation tasks. The results show
EL-attention speeds up existing models by 1.6x to 5.3x without accuracy loss.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.04779v2.pdf},
 author = {Yu Yan and Jiusheng Chen and Weizhen Qi and Nikhil Bhendawade and Yeyun Gong and Nan Duan and Ruofei Zhang},
 github_url = {https://github.com/pytorch/fairseq},
 title = {EL-Attention: Memory Efficient Lossless Attention for Generation},
 year = {2021}
}

@article{yu-2024-nonlocal,
 abstract = {Despite the recent popularity of attention-based neural architectures in core
AI fields like natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision (CV),
their potential in modeling complex physical systems remains under-explored.
Learning problems in physical systems are often characterized as discovering
operators that map between function spaces based on a few instances of function
pairs. This task frequently presents a severely ill-posed PDE inverse problem.
In this work, we propose a novel neural operator architecture based on the
attention mechanism, which we coin Nonlocal Attention Operator (NAO), and
explore its capability towards developing a foundation physical model. In
particular, we show that the attention mechanism is equivalent to a double
integral operator that enables nonlocal interactions among spatial tokens, with
a data-dependent kernel characterizing the inverse mapping from data to the
hidden parameter field of the underlying operator. As such, the attention
mechanism extracts global prior information from training data generated by
multiple systems, and suggests the exploratory space in the form of a nonlinear
kernel map. Consequently, NAO can address ill-posedness and rank deficiency in
inverse PDE problems by encoding regularization and achieving generalizability.
We empirically demonstrate the advantages of NAO over baseline neural models in
terms of generalizability to unseen data resolutions and system states. Our
work not only suggests a novel neural operator architecture for learning
interpretable foundation models of physical systems, but also offers a new
perspective towards understanding the attention mechanism.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.07307v1.pdf},
 author = {Yue Yu and Ning Liu and Fei Lu and Tian Gao and Siavash Jafarzadeh and Stewart Silling},
 title = {Nonlocal Attention Operator: Materializing Hidden Knowledge Towards Interpretable Physics Discovery},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{zandieh-2023-kdeformer,
 abstract = {Dot-product attention mechanism plays a crucial role in modern deep
architectures (e.g., Transformer) for sequence modeling, however, na\"ive exact
computation of this model incurs quadratic time and memory complexities in
sequence length, hindering the training of long-sequence models. Critical
bottlenecks are due to the computation of partition functions in the
denominator of softmax function as well as the multiplication of the softmax
matrix with the matrix of values. Our key observation is that the former can be
reduced to a variant of the kernel density estimation (KDE) problem, and an
efficient KDE solver can be further utilized to accelerate the latter via
subsampling-based fast matrix products. Our proposed KDEformer can approximate
the attention in sub-quadratic time with provable spectral norm bounds, while
all prior results merely provide entry-wise error bounds. Empirically, we
verify that KDEformer outperforms other attention approximations in terms of
accuracy, memory, and runtime on various pre-trained models. On BigGAN image
generation, we achieve better generative scores than the exact computation with
over $4\times$ speedup. For ImageNet classification with T2T-ViT, KDEformer
shows over $18\times$ speedup while the accuracy drop is less than $0.5\%$.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2302.02451v2.pdf},
 author = {Amir Zandieh and Insu Han and Majid Daliri and Amin Karbasi},
 github_url = {https://github.com/yitu-opensource/T2T-ViT},
 title = {KDEformer: Accelerating Transformers via Kernel Density Estimation},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{ainslie-2023-gqa,
 abstract = {Multi-query attention (MQA), which only uses a single key-value head,
drastically speeds up decoder inference. However, MQA can lead to quality
degradation, and moreover it may not be desirable to train a separate model
just for faster inference. We (1) propose a recipe for uptraining existing
multi-head language model checkpoints into models with MQA using 5% of original
pre-training compute, and (2) introduce grouped-query attention (GQA), a
generalization of multi-query attention which uses an intermediate (more than
one, less than number of query heads) number of key-value heads. We show that
uptrained GQA achieves quality close to multi-head attention with comparable
speed to MQA.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.13245v3.pdf},
 author = {Joshua Ainslie and James Lee-Thorp and Michiel de Jong and Yury Zemlyanskiy and Federico Lebrón and Sumit Sanghai},
 title = {Gqa: Training generalized multi-query transformer models from multi-head checkpoints.},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{rabe-2021-self,
 abstract = {We present a very simple algorithm for attention that requires $O(1)$ memory
with respect to sequence length and an extension to self-attention that
requires $O(\log n)$ memory. This is in contrast with the frequently stated
belief that self-attention requires $O(n^2)$ memory. While the time complexity
is still $O(n^2)$, device memory rather than compute capability is often the
limiting factor on modern accelerators. Thus, reducing the memory requirements
of attention allows processing of longer sequences than might otherwise be
feasible. We provide a practical implementation for accelerators that requires
$O(\sqrt{n})$ memory, is numerically stable, and is within a few percent of the
runtime of the standard implementation of attention. We also demonstrate how to
differentiate the function while remaining memory-efficient. For sequence
length 16384, the memory overhead of self-attention is reduced by 59X for
inference and by 32X for differentiation.},

@article{vaswani-2017-attention,
 abstract = {The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or
convolutional neural networks in an encoder-decoder configuration. The best

solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions
entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be
superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly
less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014

Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to
English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762v7.pdf},
